title: DOJ Escalates Alaska Senate Probe Over Alleged 'Spoiler' Candidate Scheme
snippet: Federal prosecutors are pouring FBI resources into an investigation into whether Democrats illegally backed a second candidate named Dan Sullivan in a pivotal Alaska Senate race.
content:
WASHINGTON — With just days remaining before Tuesday's critical midterm elections, the Department of Justice is rapidly expanding federal investigations into a high-stakes US Senate race in Alaska, injecting intense political drama into a contest that could determine control of the upper chamber.

US Attorney Michael Heyman announced Friday that federal law enforcement has deployed a surge of FBI agents and prosecutors to examine allegations that Democrats orchestrated a "spoiler candidate" strategy. The probe centers on the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher whose name closely mirrors that of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

Unprecedented Federal Intervention

The federal push follows a New York Times report alleging Democratic campaign operatives secretly aided the second Sullivan to siphon votes away from the GOP incumbent. While both major political parties have historically engaged in legal maneuvers to boost third-party candidates, direct federal intervention in state-administered elections at this scale is exceedingly rare.

President Donald Trump openly claimed responsibility for initiating the legal offensive, describing the situation as "voter fraud at the highest level" during a campaign rally in Florida. Justice Department lawyers have also asked a federal court to block Alaska from certifying the Senate race results if the Republican incumbent loses due to voter confusion caused by the name overlap.

Denials and Nationwide Voting Friction

Democratic candidate Mary Peltola and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have firmly denied any involvement in recruiting the retired teacher, who similarly stated he acted independently. Despite the denials, federal prosecutors insist their inquiry is moving swiftly to safeguard the process.

The legal turmoil in Alaska comes as the administration pursues lawsuits across roughly 30 states, including a push in California over mail-in ballots that federal appeals courts have repeatedly turned back. Nevertheless, Americans are turning out in historic numbers, with early voting reaching a record 49 million ballots cast nationwide.
